# Source text
Article 36. A marriage contracted by any party who, at the time of the celebration, was psychologically incapacitated to comply with the essential marital obligations of marriage, shall likewise be void even if such incapacity becomes manifest only after its solemnization.

Article 147 (first sentence). When a man and a woman who are capacitated to marry each other, live exclusively with each other as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage or under a void marriage, their wages and salaries shall be owned by them in equal shares and the property acquired by both of them through their work or industry shall be governed by the rules on co-ownership.

From Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026, quoting Tan-Andal v. Andal, G.R. No. 196359, May 11, 2021: "psychological incapacity consists of clear acts of dysfunctionality that show a lack of understanding and concomitant compliance with one's essential marital obligations due to psychic causes."

From Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026: "There is likewise no rule requiring that an expert must personally interview both spouses for the testimony to be admissible or credible."

From Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026: "The partition of the co-owned properties is not a precondition, but is merely incidental to, and is a consequence of, the nullity of the marriage."

# Key points for the tutor (reviewer-approved)
- Psychological incapacity is a legal concept, not a medical one. No clinical diagnosis is needed, and expert opinion is not required (Tan-Andal v. Andal, G.R. No. 196359, May 11, 2021, as restated in Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026).
- Three requisites, judged from the totality of the evidence:
  - Juridical antecedence: the incapacity existed at the celebration of the marriage, even if it showed only later.
  - Incurability in a legal, not medical, sense: so enduring with respect to the specific partner that the marriage cannot be saved.
  - Gravity: a genuinely psychic cause, not mere refusal, neglect or ordinary difficulty.
- Proof must be clear and convincing. Ordinary witnesses, including the spouse and people who knew the parties before the marriage, may prove it.
- Expert evidence is still admissible as an aid, not a controlling factor. An expert need not interview both spouses; the test is whether the opinion is anchored on reliable data.
- Weighing expert testimony and witness credibility raises questions of fact, which are generally not proper in a Rule 45 petition.
- Property of spouses in a void Art. 36 marriage who were capacitated to marry each other is governed by Art. 147 co-ownership. The court may declare nullity without ordering partition in the same case (Diño v. Diño, G.R. No. 178044, January 19, 2011, applied in Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026).

# Recitation drill: application fact pattern
Scenario: Lara files an Art. 36 petition against her husband Ben. Her only expert, a psychiatrist, interviewed Lara and Ben's childhood friend but never met Ben. Ben argues that the expert's opinion is worthless because she never interviewed him. Is Ben correct?
Model answer: No. Under Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026, no rule requires an expert to personally interview both spouses for the testimony to be admissible or credible. Since Tan-Andal v. Andal, G.R. No. 196359, May 11, 2021, expert opinion is not even required. What matters is whether the opinion rests on reliable data, such as testimony and observed behavior, linked to juridical antecedence, incurability and gravity, and whether the totality of the evidence is clear and convincing.

# Problem drill: exam or bar-style problem
Problem: (Original problem based on Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026. Past Bar years on Art. 36: reviewer to confirm.) Marco and Tess married in 2010 because Tess was pregnant. Friends testified that even before the wedding, Marco never decided anything without his mother, avoided every serious conversation, and showed no interest in Tess's pregnancy. After the wedding they lived with Marco's mother. Marco stayed silent whenever his mother overruled Tess, even on how to discipline their son. They stopped sharing a bed in 2013 and lived separate lives under one roof. There was no violence and no infidelity. Tess filed a petition under Art. 36. The Republic opposed, arguing: (a) there is no medical diagnosis, and the psychiatrist who testified never interviewed Marco; and (b) the marriage failed only because of ordinary in-law conflict and neglect. Tess also asked that the court first liquidate their condominium unit, bought from both their salaries, before declaring the nullity. Rule on the petition and on the property issue.
Model answer:
(Answer) The petition should be granted and the marriage declared void under Art. 36. The court need not partition the condominium unit before declaring the nullity.

(Legal basis) Art. 36, Family Code. Psychological incapacity is a legal, not a medical, concept; it needs no clinical diagnosis or expert opinion, but must show juridical antecedence, legal incurability and gravity by clear and convincing evidence (Tan-Andal v. Andal, G.R. No. 196359, May 11, 2021). An expert need not interview both spouses (Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026). Property of spouses in a void marriage who were capacitated to marry each other is co-owned under Art. 147, and partition is merely incidental to, not a precondition of, the nullity (Diño v. Diño, G.R. No. 178044, January 19, 2011; Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026).

(Application) Friends who knew Marco before the wedding described his total dependence on his mother and his emotional absence, so the incapacity existed at the celebration (juridical antecedence). Years of the same pattern toward Tess, ending in separate lives, show a condition so enduring toward this partner that the marriage cannot be repaired (incurability). It is rooted in Marco's personality structure, not a passing quarrel with in-laws (gravity). The Republic's first objection fails because no diagnosis is required and the lack of a personal interview does not by itself defeat the expert's opinion. The absence of violence or infidelity does not matter; the court looks at the totality of the evidence. The condominium unit, bought from both their salaries, is co-owned under Art. 147; the parties may partition it by agreement or in a separate proceeding.

(Conclusion) Declare the marriage void ab initio under Art. 36, and leave partition of the co-owned condominium unit to agreement or a separate action.

# Objective and multiple-choice quiz (Year 1-2)
Q (multiple choice): After Tan-Andal v. Andal, G.R. No. 196359, May 11, 2021, how is psychological incapacity under Art. 36 best described?
A) A mental illness that must be clinically diagnosed
B) A personality disorder that only an expert can prove
C) A legal concept that may be proven even without expert opinion
D) Any refusal to perform marital obligations
Correct: C
Hint: The Court moved away from treating it as a medical illness.
Hint: Ordinary witnesses can now prove it.
Why: Tan-Andal, restated in Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026, holds that psychological incapacity is a legal concept and that expert opinion is not required.

Q (multiple choice): In Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026, what did the Court say about an expert who did not personally interview one spouse?
A) The expert's testimony is inadmissible
B) No rule requires an interview of both spouses; the opinion may still be credible
C) The petition must be dismissed
D) A second expert must interview the other spouse
Correct: B
Hint: The Court called an interview of both spouses ideal, but not indispensable.
Hint: The test is whether the opinion rests on reliable data.
Why: The Court held that no rule requires an expert to personally interview both spouses for the testimony to be admissible or credible.

Q (objective): Art. 36 requires that the psychological incapacity existed at the time of the ______ of the marriage, even if it becomes manifest only later. (One word.)
Accept: celebration
Hint: The same word appears in the article: "at the time of the ...".
Why: Art. 36 voids a marriage of a party who, at the time of the celebration, was psychologically incapacitated, even if the incapacity becomes manifest only after solemnization.

Q (objective): Name the requisite of psychological incapacity that means the incapacity already existed when the marriage was celebrated. (Two words.)
Accept: juridical antecedence | antecedence
Hint: The first word relates to law; the second means "coming before".
Why: Juridical antecedence means the incapacity existed at the celebration of the marriage, even if it showed only later (Soto v. Reyes-Soto, G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026).
